strengths: Addresses an underexplored and practically important problem: how embodied agents utilize episodic memory to interpret personalized instructions, distinct from prior work on static instruction-following or semantic/procedural memory.

The two-stage (acquisition/utilization) evaluation design is a clean and well-motivated methodology that isolates memory-utilization ability from raw task-execution/reasoning capability by holding the scene and goal constant while varying instructions.
Thoughtful taxonomy of personalized knowledge (object semantics vs. user patterns, with meaningful subcategories) that enables fine-grained analysis of where models fail.

Comprehensive experiments across six LLMs (proprietary and open-source, multiple sizes), with multiple complementary analyses: knowledge-type breakdown, top-k retrieval sensitivity, memory-quality/trajectory-format ablation, and robustness to ambiguous instructions.
Includes a validation experiment (Section 4.4) confirming the framework's utilization-stage instructions are genuinely difficult without memory access, lending credibility to the benchmark's design.

Rich qualitative case study taxonomy (success/failure modes such as hallucination, missed personalization cues, inaccurate recall, over-reliance on commonsense) that provides actionable insight for future memory-system design.
Reasonably detailed documentation of dataset construction, quality control, and prompts, aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: The dataset is fairly small (438 episodes across 12 scenes), and the joint-memory task subset is especially small (36 episodes, about 12 per pairing type), limiting statistical robustness of some subcategory-level findings.

The benchmark is purely diagnostic/evaluative; no new memory architecture, retrieval method, or mitigation strategy is proposed to address the identified limitations, despite related work surveying several such systems (A-Mem, MemGPT, MemoryBank, etc.) that could have been benchmarked.
Personalized knowledge and instructions are generated by GPT-4o itself, which could introduce stylistic biases favoring GPT-4o's own comprehension and potentially confound cross-model comparisons.

The use of oracle low-level skills and text-only observations (no visual perception) sidesteps significant real-world embodied challenges, so claims about embodied agents are somewhat narrower than implied; this is acknowledged but still limits significance.
Experiments are confined to a single simulator (Habitat 3.0) and a single robot embodiment (Spot), raising questions about generalizability of findings to other platforms and environments.

The memory retrieval setup (top-k with forced inclusion of the correct memory) is somewhat artificial and does not fully reflect realistic retrieval failure scenarios, making some conclusions about memory utilization partially conflated with retrieval design choices made by the authors.

Several core findings (performance degrades with more distractor memories, multi-step routines are harder than single-object recall) are somewhat expected outcomes and offer limited surprising insight beyond confirming intuitive difficulty of the task design.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly articulated problem: memory utilization for personalization in embodied agents is under-explored, and the paper convincingly argues why conventional embodied benchmarks miss this dimension.

The MEMENTO framework's two-stage (acquisition/utilization) design with shared scene/goal but varied instructions is a clever and rigorous way to isolate memory utilization capability from other confounds (perception, low-level control), enabling clean quantification via delta metrics.

Comprehensive evaluation across 6 LLMs (proprietary and open-source, varying sizes) reveals consistent and interesting findings: object semantics recall is relatively robust while user pattern (sequential) recall is fragile, and this pattern holds across all models.

Thorough follow-up analyses (RQ2) diagnosing specific bottlenecks -- information overload with increasing top-k, and coordination failures in joint-memory tasks -- are well-designed and provide actionable insight beyond a simple leaderboard-style benchmark paper.

The proposed hierarchical knowledge-graph user-profile memory module is a reasonable, well-motivated architectural response to the diagnosed problems (separating personalized knowledge from episodic trajectory noise while retaining ICL benefits), and shows substantial improvements across single- and joint-memory tasks and across all tested models.

Extensive appendix material: dataset construction details, quality control (heuristic filtering + inter-rater reliability with Krippendorff's alpha), human baseline study, retrieval strategy ablations, robustness to noisy/partial memory, real-world scenario extensions (3-joint memory, ambiguous instructions, generalization) substantially strengthen the empirical rigor and demonstrate the authors considered many angles.

Good qualitative error taxonomy (Figure 5) illuminating specific failure modes (commonsense override, missed personalization cues, inaccurate recall) that adds interpretability to the quantitative results.
Reasonable ethics/reproducibility statements and plan to release code/data.
weaknesses: The evaluation relies on oracle perception and motor skills, isolating a single (LLM planning) layer of the embodied agent stack; while explicitly acknowledged as a limitation, this significantly narrows the claims' applicability to real embodied deployments where perception and low-level control errors dominate.

The benchmark is built entirely on synthetic, LLM-generated (GPT-4o) personalized knowledge and instructions rather than real human-authored personalization data, which may not fully capture the diversity, ambiguity, and idiosyncrasy of genuine user preferences; this could bias results toward patterns GPT-4o itself finds easy/hard to generate and interpret, creating potential circularity since GPT-4o is also one of the evaluated agents.

Dataset scale is fairly modest (201 base episodes, only 36 joint-memory episodes across three pair types, i.e., 12 each), which limits statistical power especially for the joint-memory and extended analyses (3-joint memory with only 41 tasks, ambiguous instruction experiments with only 30 tasks).
The human baseline study is very small (4 participants, 20 tasks) and mainly serves to confirm solvability rather than provide a robust quantitative human performance comparison.

The user-profile memory module's construction and retrieval pipeline itself heavily relies on LLM calls (extraction, resolution of add/update, reformulation), so its benefits may partly reflect additional LLM inference/test-time compute rather than a purely architectural insight; the paper does not fully control for or discuss this additional compute/inference cost when comparing to baselines.

Some findings, while interesting, are somewhat expected given prior literature on long-context degradation and in-context learning (e.g., information overload with more retrieved memories, degradation from summarization for smaller models), reducing the novelty of certain sub-claims even though the embodied-personalization framing is new.

The knowledge graph update/retrieval algorithms (Algorithms 1-2) are described at a fairly high level without deep ablation on graph design choices (e.g., sensitivity to LLM used for resolution, error propagation from incorrect add/update decisions), leaving some architectural design decisions under-justified.

The paper's core contribution (a benchmark plus a proposed but still LLM-heavy memory architecture) is incremental relative to a growing body of memory-augmented LLM agent work (MemGPT, A-Mem, Generative Agents) cited in the extended related work section; the paper could better position its architectural novelty against these existing memory frameworks beyond the embodied-specific application.
